planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil; Myrtifolia is an old, slow-growing English boxwood selection with narrow, myrtle-like leaves distinctly finer than typical sempervirens foliage.

directions: Myrtifolia is a long-cultivated dwarf English boxwood sport named for its small, narrow, myrtle-like leaves, which give the shrub a noticeably finer, more delicate texture than the broad-leaved species. Growth is dense and compact but very slow, producing a tidy rounded mound that needs only occasional light shearing to stay neat over many decades. Its refined foliage makes it a good choice for small-scale formal edging, knot gardens, and container specimens where an especially fine-textured boxwood is wanted. Provide good air circulation and well-drained soil to reduce the risk of boxwood blight and leafminer common to old English boxwood plantings.

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil; Salicifolia is an old European boxwood selection grown for its long, narrow, willow-like leaves and looser, more upright habit than typical rounded boxwood forms.

directions: Salicifolia, sometimes offered as 'Angustifolia', is an heirloom English boxwood grown chiefly for its elongated, narrow, willow-shaped leaves that hang with a looser, slightly weeping grace absent from the compact rounded cultivars. Its habit is more upright and open than typical hedging boxwoods, so it reads better as an unclipped specimen or informal screen than as a tightly sheared edge. The narrow foliage catches breezes and light differently than broad-leaved sempervirens forms, adding textural contrast among darker, denser boxwood plantings. Grow in well-drained soil with reliable air movement, and watch for boxwood leafminer and blight as with other English boxwood selections.

common_name: National Boxwood (Upright New Zealand Hedging Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in well-drained soil; National is an upright, densely branching boxwood selection widely grown in New Zealand and Australia for uniform clipped hedges and topiary.

directions: National is a narrow, upright boxwood selection favored in Southern Hemisphere gardens for its consistent, dense branching, which produces uniform clipped hedges and formal shapes with fewer gaps than seedling-grown boxwood. Its compact, columnar-leaning habit needs less lateral space than spreading sempervirens forms, making it useful for tight parterres, low walls of clipped foliage, and repeated topiary shapes along a formal path. Regular shearing two to three times during the growing season keeps the dense surface characteristic of well-maintained hedging boxwood. Provide good drainage and airflow, since dense, closely clipped plantings of any boxwood cultivar are more prone to blight in humid weather.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil; Blauer Heinz is a German-raised boxwood selection valued for its glaucous, blue-gray-green foliage and dependable cold hardiness.

directions: Blauer Heinz (German for 'Blue Heinz') is a cold-hardy boxwood selection bred in Germany, distinguished by a subtle blue-gray cast over its small, dense leaves that stays more pronounced through winter than the plain green of most sempervirens forms. Its compact, mounded habit and steady growth rate suit low hedging, foundation plantings, and mixed borders where a cooler-toned evergreen accent is wanted alongside gold- or white-variegated companions. It was selected in part for reliable winter color retention in Central European climates, making it a good option for colder gardens seeking an alternative to English boxwood. Provide well-drained soil and good air circulation, and monitor for boxwood leafminer and blight as with any sempervirens cultivar.

common_name: Copper Beauty Witch Hazel (Kew-Raised Coppery-Orange Winter Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Copper Beauty is a Kew Gardens-raised hybrid witch hazel selected for its coppery-orange petals set against reddish calyces.

directions: Copper Beauty is a hybrid witch hazel raised at the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, prized for its warm coppery-orange, strap-like petals that unfurl on bare branches in mid to late winter above rusty-red calyces, giving a richer, more smoldering color effect than the cooler yellows of many intermedia cultivars. It grows into a broad, vase-shaped shrub with oval leaves that turn attractive shades of orange and red in autumn, offering two distinct seasons of color from a single specimen. Site it where low winter light can pass through the flowers, such as against a dark evergreen backdrop, and provide moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun. Prune lightly after flowering only to remove crossing or damaged wood, since witch hazels flower best with minimal interference to their natural branching.

common_name: Ostergold Witch Hazel (Easter Gold Early-Season Yellow Witch Hazel)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Ostergold (German for 'Easter Gold') is a German-raised hybrid witch hazel selected for clear yellow flowers opening earlier in the winter season than many intermedia cultivars.

directions: Ostergold is a German-raised hybrid witch hazel named for its clear, bright yellow, ribbon-like petals, which typically open on bare stems earlier in the winter-to-spring window than many other yellow-flowered intermedia cultivars, extending the witch hazel display into the coldest part of the season. It develops an upright, vase-shaped form with mid-green leaves that turn gold-yellow in autumn, echoing the flower color for a cohesive seasonal effect. Plant it in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun, ideally where late-winter sun can backlight the flowers against a darker backdrop. Minimal pruning is needed beyond removing dead or crossing wood after bloom, since witch hazels resent heavy shearing.

common_name: Adonis Witch Hazel (Compact Upright Orange-Red Dutch Witch Hazel)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Adonis is a Dutch-raised hybrid witch hazel with a more compact, upright habit than many intermedia cultivars, bearing curled orange-red petals in winter.

directions: Adonis is a Dutch-bred hybrid witch hazel with a noticeably more compact, upright habit than many intermedia cultivars, making it a good fit for smaller gardens where full-size selections would eventually crowd the space. Its narrow, curled petals open in shades of orange-red on bare branches during the winter months, carrying the light, spicy fragrance typical of the group, and its oval leaves turn warm autumn tones before dropping. Grow it in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun, and give it room to develop its upright vase shape without being crowded by larger shrubs. Prune only lightly after flowering to remove damaged or crossing wood, preserving the naturally tidy branching that suits its smaller garden scale.
